name: Matthew
sourceNote: Translated from the Greek text of B. F. Westcott and F. J. A. Hort, *The New Testament in the Original Greek* (1881; public domain), in the public-domain electronic edition of Maurice A. Robinson, with Tischendorf’s eighth edition (1869–72; public domain) consulted. Variant readings were also compared with the SBL Greek New Testament, the Nestle–Aland *Novum Testamentum Graece*, and the Byzantine text of Robinson and Pierpont, which were consulted for variants only. Early papyri containing parts of Matthew include P1, P45, P64/67 and P104 (2nd–3rd centuries); where they are cited in the notes, their readings are reported from the standard editions and have not been verified against the manuscripts. Passages found in later manuscripts but absent from the earliest witnesses (6:13b; 17:21; 18:11; 23:14) keep their traditional verse numbers, and their text is given in the notes. Greek *kyrios* is rendered “Lord”; where it stands for the divine name in an Old Testament quotation or phrase, a note says so. Old Testament quotations are translated afresh from the Greek of Matthew, with the source given in a note. Money, measures and times of day are given in modern terms in the text (for example, a denarius as “a day’s wage”), with the original term in a note. The Gospel is anonymous; from the second century it has been attributed to Matthew the tax collector (9:9; 10:3). Most scholars date it about AD 80–90 and hold that its author used the Gospel of Mark; others date it before AD 70.

verses.text: The record of the origins{a} of Jesus the Messiah,{b} the son of David, the son of Abraham.
Abraham was father to Isaac, Isaac father to Jacob, and Jacob father to Judah and his brothers.{c}
Judah was father to Perez and Zerah by Tamar, Perez father to Hezron, and Hezron father to Ram.{d}
Ram was father to Amminadab, Amminadab father to Nahshon, and Nahshon father to Salmon.
Salmon was father to Boaz by Rahab, Boaz father to Obed by Ruth, and Obed father to Jesse.
Jesse was father to David the king. David was father to Solomon by the woman who had been Uriah’s wife.
Solomon was father to Rehoboam, Rehoboam father to Abijah, and Abijah father to Asa.{e}
Asa was father to Jehoshaphat, Jehoshaphat father to Joram, and Joram father to Uzziah.{f}
Uzziah was father to Jotham, Jotham father to Ahaz, and Ahaz father to Hezekiah.
Hezekiah was father to Manasseh, Manasseh father to Amon,{g} and Amon father to Josiah.
Josiah was father to Jechoniah{h} and his brothers in the time of the exile to Babylon.
After the exile to Babylon, Jechoniah was father to Shealtiel, and Shealtiel father to Zerubbabel.
Zerubbabel was father to Abiud, Abiud father to Eliakim, and Eliakim father to Azor.
Azor was father to Zadok, Zadok father to Achim, and Achim father to Eliud.
Eliud was father to Eleazar, Eleazar father to Matthan, and Matthan father to Jacob.
Jacob was father to Joseph the husband of Mary,{i} and from her was born Jesus, who is called Messiah.
So the generations from Abraham to David were fourteen in all; from David to the exile to Babylon, fourteen generations; and from the exile to Babylon to the Messiah, fourteen generations.{j}

The birth of Jesus the Messiah happened like this. His mother Mary had been promised in marriage to Joseph, and before they came together it became evident that she was carrying a child from the Holy Spirit.
Joseph her husband was a just man, and because he did not wish to make a public example of her, he made up his mind to release her from the marriage in secret.{k}

But while he was weighing these things, an angel of the Lord{l} appeared to him in a dream and said, “Joseph, son of David, have no fear about taking Mary to be your wife, because what has been conceived in her comes from the Holy Spirit.
She will give birth to a son, and you shall give him the name Jesus, because he is the one who will save his people from their sins.”{m}
All of this took place so that the word spoken by the Lord through the prophet would be fulfilled:
“Look, the virgin will become pregnant and will give birth to a son, and they will call his name Emmanuel,”{n} a name that means, when translated, “God with us.”
When Joseph awoke from his sleep, he did what the angel of the Lord had directed him to do, and took his wife into his home.
Yet he did not have relations with her{o} until she had given birth to a son; and he gave him the name Jesus.

notes.text: The record of the origins: Greek *biblos geneseōs*, “book of the genesis,” the phrase used in the Greek Old Testament at Gen 2:4 and 5:1. It may introduce the genealogy alone (1:1–17) or the whole account of Jesus’ beginnings.

Jesus the Messiah: *Jesus* is the Greek form of the Hebrew *Yeshua* (*Yehoshua*, Joshua), “Yahweh saves” (see 1:21). *Messiah* translates Greek *Christos*, “Anointed One,” the equivalent of Hebrew *mashiach*. In this translation *Christos* is rendered “Messiah” where it functions as a title, as it usually does in the Gospels, and “Christ” where it has become part of Jesus’ name.
The meanings of the Old Testament names in this genealogy are given in the notes at their first appearance in the Old Testament. Compare the genealogies in Ruth 4:18–22 and 1 Chr 1–3.

Ram: Greek *Aram*, the Greek Old Testament’s spelling of Hebrew *Ram* (Ruth 4:19; 1 Chr 2:9–10). Likewise *Nahshon* (Greek *Naassōn*), *Hezron* (*Esrōm*), *Uzziah* (*Ozias*) and others are given in their Old Testament forms.

Asa: the Westcott–Hort text, with the earliest manuscripts (Sinaiticus, Vaticanus), reads *Asaph*, the name of the psalmist; later manuscripts read *Asa*, the name of the king (1 Kgs 15:8). *Asaph* may be the evangelist’s own spelling or an early slip; the king is clearly meant. Scholarly review recommended.

Joram … Uzziah: three kings, Ahaziah, Joash and Amaziah, stand between Joram and Uzziah in 1 Chr 3:11–12; the genealogy omits them, probably to arrive at three sets of fourteen (1:17). Uzziah is also called Azariah (2 Kgs 15:1).
Amon: the Westcott–Hort text, with Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, reads *Amos*; later manuscripts read *Amon*, the name of the king (2 Kgs 21:18). As in verse 7, the king is meant.
Jechoniah: also called Jehoiachin (2 Kgs 24:6–15). His father Jehoiakim is not named; Jechoniah was Josiah’s grandson (1 Chr 3:15–16).
Joseph … Mary: *Joseph* means “may he add” (Gen 30:24). *Mary* (Greek *Maria* or *Mariam*) is the Hebrew name *Miriam* (Exod 15:20); its meaning is uncertain.

Fourteen generations: the three groups are arranged deliberately. It has been suggested that fourteen is the numerical value of the name *David* in Hebrew (D = 4, W = 6, D = 4); this is reported, not certain.

Release her from the marriage in secret: Jewish betrothal was a binding legal commitment, already called marriage (Joseph is her “husband”), and could be ended only by divorce. Joseph planned a private divorce rather than a public accusation.
An angel of the Lord: in the Old Testament, “the angel of Yahweh.” The Greek *kyrios* (“Lord”) here stands for the divine name, as also in 1:22, 24 and 2:13, 15, 19.
Jesus … save: the name *Jesus* (*Yeshua*) means “Yahweh saves”; the angel’s words play on its meaning.

Isa 7:14, quoted in the wording of the Greek Old Testament, which has *parthenos*, “virgin”; the Hebrew has *ʿalmah*, “young woman.” *Emmanuel* (Hebrew *ʿImmanu ʾEl*) means “God is with us” (Isa 8:8, 10).
Did not have relations with her: literally “did not know her,” the biblical idiom for sexual union.

verses.text: Now after Jesus was born in Bethlehem{a} of Judea in the days of Herod the king,{b} there came to Jerusalem magi{c} from the regions of the east,
They kept asking, “Where is the one born to be king of the Jews? We watched his star rise{d} and have come here to bow down to him.”
When King Herod heard this he was deeply troubled, and all Jerusalem with him.
He called together all the chief priests and scribes{e} of the people and pressed them to tell him where the Messiah was to be born.
They told him, “In Bethlehem of Judea, for this is what the prophet wrote:
‘And you, Bethlehem, in Judah’s land, are in no way the least among Judah’s leading towns; out of you will come forth a ruler, one who will be shepherd of my people Israel.’ ”{f}
Then Herod summoned the magi in secret and learned from them exactly when the star had appeared.
Then he sent them on to Bethlehem, saying, “Go, make a careful search for the child, and when you have found him, report to me, so that I may also come and bow before him.”
After listening to the king they set out, and the star they had seen at its rising went ahead of them until it came and stopped over the place where the child was.
When they saw the star, their joy knew no bounds.

Going into the house, they saw the child with Mary his mother, and they fell down and paid him homage. Then they opened their treasure chests and presented him with gifts: gold, frankincense, and myrrh.{g}
Then, warned in a dream not to return to Herod, they went back to their own land by another route.

When they had left, Joseph saw in a dream an angel of the Lord, who told him, “Get up, take the child and his mother, and escape to Egypt. Stay there until I tell you, because Herod is going to look for the child in order to kill him.”
So Joseph got up, took the child and his mother by night, and withdrew to Egypt.
He remained there until Herod died. This was to fulfill what the Lord had spoken through the prophet: “Out of Egypt I called my son.”{h}

Herod, realizing that the magi had made a fool of him, was furious. He gave orders to put to death every boy in Bethlehem and all its surrounding district who was two years of age or younger, reckoning from the time he had carefully learned from the magi.
Then what had been spoken through Jeremiah the prophet was fulfilled:
“A voice was heard in Ramah, weeping and loud lament: Rachel weeping for her children; and she would not be comforted, because they are no more.”{i}
But when Herod had died, an angel of the Lord appeared in a dream to Joseph in Egypt
and said, “Get up, take the child and his mother, and go to the land of Israel, because those who sought the child’s life are dead.”
So he got up, took the child and his mother, and went into the land of Israel.
But when he heard that Archelaus{j} was reigning over Judea in place of his father Herod, he was afraid to go there. Having been warned in a dream, he withdrew to the region of Galilee{k}
and went and settled in a town called Nazareth.{l} This was to fulfill what had been spoken through the prophets: “He will be called a Nazarene.”

notes.text: Bethlehem: “house of bread,” the town of David, about 6 miles (10 km) south of Jerusalem.
Herod the king: Herod the Great, appointed king of Judea by the Roman Senate, who reigned 37–4 BC. Jesus was therefore born before 4 BC. The name *Herod* probably means “heroic.”

Magi: Greek *magoi*, originally a Persian priestly class; by this period the word was used for experts in astrology and the interpretation of dreams. The text does not call them kings or give their number.
When it rose: or “in the east.” The Greek *en tē anatolē* can mean either; here and in 2:9 it probably refers to the star’s rising.
Scribes: experts in the Law of Moses who taught and interpreted it.
Mic 5:2 (5:1 in Hebrew), freely combined with 2 Sam 5:2. Where Micah has “who are small among the clans of Judah,” the quotation reads “by no means least.”
Gold, frankincense, and myrrh: costly gifts. Frankincense is a fragrant resin burned as incense; myrrh is an aromatic resin used in perfume and in burial (John 19:39). Compare Isa 60:6; Ps 72:10–11.
Hos 11:1, translated from the Hebrew; the Greek Old Testament reads “his children.” In Hosea the “son” is Israel, brought out of Egypt in the exodus.

Jer 31:15 (38:15 in the Greek Old Testament). Ramah lay about 5 miles (8 km) north of Jerusalem, near the traditional tomb of Rachel; Jeremiah pictures Rachel, the mother of Joseph and Benjamin, mourning the exiles.
Archelaus: son of Herod the Great, who ruled Judea, Samaria and Idumea from 4 BC until Rome deposed him for brutality in AD 6.
Galilee: from Hebrew *galil*, “circle” or “district,” the northern region of the land west of the Sea of Galilee, then ruled by Herod Antipas.

Nazareth … Nazarene: Nazareth, a small village in the hills of lower Galilee, is not mentioned in the Old Testament, and no prophetic text contains the words quoted. Matthew may be playing on Hebrew *netser*, “branch,” the messianic shoot of Isa 11:1, or on the Nazirite of Judg 13:5, 7; he cites “the prophets” in general. Scholarly review recommended.

verses.text: In those days John the Baptist{a} appeared, preaching in the wilderness of Judea,
“Turn your lives around,{b} for the kingdom of heaven{c} has come near.”
He is the one of whom Isaiah the prophet spoke when he said, “A voice of one calling out in the wilderness: ‘Make ready the way of the Lord, make his paths straight.’ ”{d}
John himself wore clothing made of camel’s hair with a leather belt around his waist, and his food was locusts and wild honey.{e}
Then Jerusalem and all Judea and the whole region around the Jordan went out to him,
and confessing their sins, they were baptized by him in the Jordan River.{f}
But seeing many Pharisees and Sadducees{g} coming out for his baptism, he said to them, “Offspring of vipers! Who warned you to run from the wrath that is on its way?
Then produce fruit that fits with repentance.
And do not suppose you can say among yourselves, ‘Abraham is our father,’ for I tell you that God can raise up children for Abraham out of these stones.
Already the ax is lying at the root of the trees; every tree, then, that fails to bear good fruit is chopped down and tossed into the fire.

“For my part, I baptize you in water for repentance; but the one coming after me is stronger than I, and I am unworthy even to carry his sandals. He himself will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire.
His winnowing fork is in his hand, and he will clear his threshing floor completely; his wheat he will gather into the barn, but the chaff he will burn up in a fire that cannot be put out.”
Then Jesus arrived from Galilee at the Jordan to be baptized by John.
But John tried to stop him, saying, “It is I who need to be baptized by you, and yet you come to me?”
Jesus answered him, “Let it be so for now. It is right for us in this way to carry out all that God requires.”{h} Then John consented.
And as soon as Jesus had been baptized, he came up out of the water, and at that moment the heavens were opened,{i} and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and coming upon him.
And a voice out of the heavens said, “This is my Son, the one I love; with him I am well pleased.”{j}

notes.text: John the Baptist: *John* is the Greek form of Hebrew *Yohanan*, “Yahweh has been gracious.” *The Baptist* (literally “the one who immerses”) is a title describing his ministry.
Turn your lives around: Greek *metanoeite*, traditionally “repent,” a call to a complete change of mind and direction. The noun *metanoia* in 3:8, 11 is rendered “repentance.”

The kingdom of heaven: Matthew’s usual phrase for “the kingdom of God” (the expression found in Mark and Luke), following the Jewish custom of speaking reverently of God by referring to heaven. It means God’s rule as king.

Isa 40:3, in the wording of the Greek Old Testament. In the Hebrew text, “the Lord” is Yahweh, and “make his paths straight” reads “make straight in the desert a highway for our God.” The Hebrew can also be punctuated, “A voice is calling: In the wilderness prepare …”
Clothing of camel’s hair … leather belt: the dress of Elijah (2 Kgs 1:8; compare Mal 4:5). Locusts were permitted food under the Law (Lev 11:22).
Jordan River: from Hebrew *Yarden*, probably “the one that goes down.”

Pharisees and Sadducees: the Pharisees (probably “separated ones”) were a lay movement devoted to strict observance of the Law and its traditions; the Sadducees (probably named after Zadok, the high priest under David and Solomon) were a priestly aristocracy who accepted only the written Law and denied the resurrection (22:23).
To carry out all that God requires: literally “to fulfill all righteousness.”
The heavens were opened: the Westcott–Hort text, with Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, lacks “to him” after “opened,” which most later manuscripts include.
This is my Son … well pleased: compare Ps 2:7; Isa 42:1; Gen 22:2. *The one I love*: or “my beloved,” “my only Son.”

verses.text: Then Jesus was led up by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tested{a} by the devil.{b}
After going without food for forty days and forty nights, he was famished.
The tempter came to him and said, “Since you are the Son of God, order these stones to turn into loaves of bread.”
But he answered, “Scripture says, ‘Not by bread alone will a person live, but by every word that goes out from the mouth of God.’ ”{c}
Next the devil took him into the holy city and placed him on the highest point{d} of the temple,

and said to him, “If you are God’s Son, throw yourself down from here, for Scripture says, ‘He will command his angels concerning you,’ and ‘On their hands they will bear you up, so that you never strike your foot against a stone.’ ”{e}
Jesus told him, “It is also written, ‘You must not test the Lord your God.’ ”{f}
Once more the devil took him up to an exceedingly high mountain and showed him all the kingdoms of the world and their splendor,
and he said to him, “All of this I will give you, if you will bow down and worship me.”
Then Jesus answered him, “Away with you, Satan!{g} For it is written, ‘The Lord your God you shall worship, and him alone you shall serve.’ ”{h}
Then the devil let him alone, and angels came and attended to him.
When Jesus heard that John had been handed over,{i} he withdrew into Galilee.
He left Nazareth and settled in Capernaum,{j} the lakeside town in the districts of Zebulun and Naphtali,
so that what was spoken through Isaiah the prophet might be fulfilled:
“Land of Zebulun, land of Naphtali, the way of the sea, beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the Gentiles:{k}
the people sitting in darkness have seen a great light, and on those sitting in the region and shadow of death a light has dawned.”{l}
From then on Jesus began to preach and to say, “Turn your lives around, for the kingdom of heaven has come near.”
As he was walking along beside the Sea of Galilee, he saw two brothers, Simon, who is called Peter, and Andrew his brother,{m} casting a net into the lake, for they were fishermen.
He said to them, “Come, follow me, and I will make you fishers of people.”
At once they left their nets behind and followed him.
Going on from there, he saw two other brothers, James the son of Zebedee and John his brother,{n} in the boat with their father Zebedee, mending their nets; and he called them.
At once they left the boat and their father and followed him.
Jesus went about all over Galilee, teaching in their synagogues,{o} proclaiming the good news{p} of the kingdom, and healing every disease and every ailment among the people.

Word about him spread through all Syria, and people brought to him all who were ill, those in the grip of various diseases and pains, those under the power of demons, epileptics,{q} and the paralyzed; and he healed them.
And great crowds followed him from Galilee and the Ten Towns,{r} from Jerusalem and Judea, and from the land beyond the Jordan.

notes.text: Tested: Greek *peirazō* can mean “test” or “tempt.”
The devil: Greek *diabolos*, “slanderer,” the Greek Old Testament’s word for Hebrew *satan*.
Deut 8:3. The forty days recall Israel’s forty years in the wilderness and Moses’ forty days on the mountain (Exod 34:28; Deut 9:9).
Highest point: Greek *pterygion*, “little wing,” perhaps a corner of the temple’s outer wall high above the Kidron Valley. The exact location is uncertain.
Ps 91:11–12 (90:11–12 in the Greek Old Testament).
Deut 6:16. In the Hebrew text, “the Lord your God” is “Yahweh your God,” as also in 4:10.
Satan: Hebrew for “adversary” or “accuser.” Some later manuscripts add “Get behind me” (as in 16:23); the Westcott–Hort text lacks it.
Deut 6:13. The Hebrew has “You shall fear Yahweh your God and serve him”; Jesus’ wording follows the Greek Old Testament with “worship” and “alone.”
Handed over: that is, arrested and put in prison (see 14:3–4).
Capernaum: Greek form of Hebrew *Kefar Nahum*, “village of Nahum,” a town on the northwest shore of the Sea of Galilee.
Galilee of the nations: or “of the Gentiles”; the Greek *ethnē* means non-Jewish peoples.
Isa 9:1–2 (8:23–9:1 in Hebrew), quoted freely.

Simon … Peter … Andrew: *Simon* is the Greek form of Hebrew *Shimʿon* (Simeon), “one who hears” (Gen 29:33). *Peter*, Greek *Petros*, means “rock” (see 16:18). *Andrew* is a Greek name meaning “manly.”
James … John: *James* is the English form of the Greek *Iakōbos*, that is, *Jacob* (“heel-grabber” or “he supplants,” Gen 25:26). *Zebedee* is from Hebrew *Zavdi*, “my gift” or “gift of Yahweh.”
Synagogues: Greek *synagōgē*, “gathering,” the local Jewish assembly for prayer and the reading and teaching of Scripture, and the building where it met.
Good news: Greek *euangelion*, traditionally “gospel.”
Epileptics: literally “moonstruck,” a term that reflected an ancient belief that seizures were caused by the moon.
The Ten Towns: Greek *Dekapolis*, a league of largely Gentile cities, most of them east of the Jordan.

verses.text: When he saw the crowds, he went up the mountain, and after he had sat down, his disciples came to him.
and he began to teach them. He said:
“Blessed{a} are those who are poor in spirit, since theirs is the kingdom of heaven.
Blessed are those who grieve, for they will be comforted.
Blessed are the gentle, for the earth will be their inheritance.{b}
Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they will be filled to the full.
Blessed are those who show mercy, for mercy will be shown to them.
Blessed are the pure in heart, since it is they who will see God.
Blessed are those who make peace, for they will be called sons of God.
Blessed are those who have been persecuted for the sake of righteousness, for the kingdom of heaven belongs to them.
“You are blessed when people insult you, harass you, and tell all kinds of lies about you because of me.
Rejoice and be glad, for great is your reward in heaven; that is how they hounded the prophets who came before you.
“You are the salt of the earth. But if salt goes flat,{c} how will its saltiness be restored? It is then good for nothing except to be thrown out and walked on by people.
You are the light of the world. A town that sits on a hilltop cannot stay hidden.
Nor does anyone light a lamp and set it under a basket;{d} they put it on the lampstand, and it gives light to everyone in the house.
In the same way, let your light shine before people, so that they may see the good you do and give glory to your Father in heaven.
“Do not imagine that I came to do away with the Law or the Prophets. I did not come to do away with them but to fulfill them.
Amen,{e} I tell you, until heaven and earth pass away, not one iota, not one tiny stroke,{f} will pass away from the Law until everything has taken place.

So anyone who loosens even one of the least of these commandments, and teaches people to do likewise, will be named least in the kingdom of heaven; but anyone who obeys them and teaches them will be named great in the kingdom of heaven.
For I tell you that unless your righteousness goes far beyond that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven.
“You have heard that it was said to the people of long ago, ‘You shall not murder,’{g} and ‘Whoever murders will be liable to judgment.’

But I say to you that everyone who is angry with his brother{h} will be liable to judgment; whoever says to his brother, ‘Raca,’{i} will be liable to the high council;{j} and whoever says, ‘You fool,’ will be liable to the fire of Gehenna.{k}
So if you are offering your gift at the altar and there you recall that your brother has something against you,
leave your gift right there in front of the altar and go. First be reconciled with your brother, and then come back and offer your gift.
Come to terms quickly with your opponent at law while you are still on the way with him, or your opponent may hand you over to the judge, and the judge to the officer, and you will be put in prison.
Amen, I tell you, you will not get out of there until you have paid back the last cent.{l}
“You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall not commit adultery.’{m}
But I say to you that anyone who looks at a woman with desire for her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.
If your right eye trips you up,{n} gouge it out and fling it away. Better for you that one of your members be lost than that your entire body be cast into Gehenna.
And if your right hand trips you up, cut it off and fling it away. Better for you that one of your members be lost than that your entire body go off into Gehenna.
“It has been said too, ‘Anyone who sends away his wife is to hand her a written notice of divorce.’{o}
But I tell you, anyone who sends away his wife, other than for sexual immorality,{p} causes her to become an adulteress, and anyone who marries a woman so sent away commits adultery.
“Again, you have heard that it was said to the people of long ago, ‘You shall not break your oath, but you shall carry out the oaths you have sworn to the Lord.’{q}
But I say to you, take no oath at all, whether by heaven, because it is God’s throne,
or by the earth, because it is the footstool for his feet, or by Jerusalem, because it is the city of the great King.{r}
Nor should you swear by your head, for you cannot make one single hair white or black.
Let your speech be ‘Yes, yes’ or ‘No, no’; anything beyond that comes from the evil one.{s}
“You have heard that it was said, ‘An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth.’{t}
But I say to you, do not resist an evil person. On the contrary, whoever slaps you on the right cheek, turn the other one toward him as well.
And if someone wants to sue you and take your shirt,{u} let him have your cloak as well.
And whoever forces you to go one mile,{v} go two with him.
Give to the one who asks you, and do not turn your back on the one who would borrow from you.
“You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy.’{w}
But I say to you, love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you,{x}
so that you may become sons of your Father in heaven; for he makes his sun rise on the evil and the good, and sends rain on those who do right and those who do wrong.
For if you love those who love you, what reward will you have? Do not even the tax collectors{y} do the same?
And if you greet only your brothers, what are you doing that is out of the ordinary? Do not even the Gentiles do the same?
You, then, are to be perfect,{z} just as your heavenly Father is perfect.

notes.text: Blessed: Greek *makarios*, “happy,” “fortunate,” in the sense of being favored by God; also in verses 4–11.
Ps 37:11. *Earth* may also be translated “land.”
Goes flat: literally “becomes foolish,” that is, loses its taste. Ancient salt from the Dead Sea region was mixed with other minerals and could lose its savor.
Basket: Greek *modios*, a container holding about 9 quarts (8.75 liters) of dry goods, used as a measuring bucket.

Amen: a Hebrew word meaning “surely,” “so be it.” Jesus uses it uniquely to introduce his own solemn statements, rather than to confirm someone else’s words. Traditionally translated “Truly” or “Verily.”
Iota … stroke: the iota is the smallest Greek letter (corresponding to Hebrew *yod*); the “stroke” (Greek *keraia*, “little horn”) is a small mark that distinguishes one Hebrew letter from another.
Exod 20:13; Deut 5:17.

Angry with his brother: many later manuscripts add “without cause”; the earliest witnesses, including P64/67 (reported), Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, lack it, and the Westcott–Hort text omits it. *Brother* here means a fellow member of the community, man or woman.
Raca: an Aramaic term of contempt, probably “empty-head.”
High council: Greek *synedrion*, the Sanhedrin, the supreme Jewish council in Jerusalem.
Gehenna: the Greek form of Hebrew *Ge Hinnom*, “Valley of Hinnom,” south of Jerusalem, once a site of child sacrifice (Jer 7:31) and later a symbol of final judgment. Traditionally translated “hell.”
Last cent: Greek *kodrantēs* (Latin *quadrans*), the smallest Roman copper coin, worth one sixty-fourth of a denarius (a day’s wage).
Exod 20:14; Deut 5:18.
Causes you to fall: Greek *skandalizō*, to cause someone to stumble into sin; also in verse 30.
Sexual immorality: Greek *porneia*, a broad term for illicit sexual conduct.
Lev 19:12; Num 30:2; Deut 23:21. In the Old Testament the oath is sworn to Yahweh.
The evil one: or “evil.” The Greek can be masculine (“the evil one,” the devil) or neuter (“evil”); also in 5:39 and 6:13.
Shirt … cloak: the *chitōn* was the long tunic worn next to the skin; the *himation* was the outer garment, which a poor person also used as a blanket at night (Exod 22:26–27).
One mile: Greek *milion*, the Roman mile of a thousand paces, about 1,620 yards (1.48 km). Roman soldiers could compel civilians to carry their baggage for this distance.
Lev 19:18. “Hate your enemy” is not found in the Old Testament; it may reflect popular understanding of the command.

Pray for those who persecute you: later manuscripts expand the verse to read “bless those who curse you, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who mistreat you and persecute you” (compare Luke 6:27–28). The Westcott–Hort text, with Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, has the shorter reading.
Tax collectors: local Jews who collected tolls and taxes for Rome or for Herod Antipas, widely despised as collaborators and for their dishonesty.
Perfect: Greek *teleios*, “complete,” “whole,” “mature”; compare Lev 19:2; Deut 18:13.

verses.text: “Be careful not to practice your righteousness in front of others in order to be seen by them; otherwise you have no reward from your Father in heaven.

“So whenever you give to the poor, do not blow a trumpet before you, as the hypocrites{a} do in the synagogues and in the streets, so as to win people’s praise. Amen, I tell you, they have their reward in full.
Rather, when you give alms, keep your left hand unaware of what your right hand does,
so that your almsgiving may stay hidden; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you.{b}

“And whenever you pray, do not be like the hypocrites; they love to stand and pray in the synagogues and on the street corners, so that people will see them. Amen, I tell you, they have their reward in full.
But you, when you pray, enter your private room, shut your door, and pray to your Father who is unseen; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you.
“When you pray, do not babble on and on as the Gentiles do, for they think that by using a great many words they will get a hearing.
So do not be like them, for your Father knows what you need before you ask him.

Pray, then, in this way:
‘Our Father, you who are in heaven,
let your name be treated as holy.

May your kingdom come,
your will be done,
on earth as it is done in heaven.
Give us today the bread we need for the day ahead;{c}

and forgive us our debts,
as we too have forgiven those who are in debt to us;{d}

and do not lead us into a time of testing,
but rescue us from the evil one.’{e}
For if you forgive others their wrongdoings, your heavenly Father will forgive you as well;
but if you do not forgive people, neither will your Father pardon your wrongdoings.
“And whenever you fast, do not look gloomy like the hypocrites, for they make their faces unsightly{f} so that people will notice they are fasting. Amen, I tell you, they have their reward in full.
But you, when you fast, anoint your head and wash your face,
so that it will not be people who notice that you are fasting, but your Father, who is in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you.
“Do not pile up for yourselves treasures on earth, where the moth and rust{g} eat them away and where burglars break in and steal.
Instead, pile up treasures for yourselves in heaven, where neither moth nor rust eats them away, and where burglars do not break in or steal.
For where your treasure is, that is where your heart will be too.
“The lamp of the body is the eye. If your eye is sound,{h} then, your whole body will be full of light;
but if your eye is diseased, your entire body will be filled with darkness. If, then, the light within you is darkness, how deep that darkness is!
“No one can be a slave to two masters; either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be loyal to one and despise the other. You cannot be a slave both to God and to wealth.{i}

“That is why I tell you, do not be anxious about your life, about what you will eat or drink, or about your body, about what you will wear. Is life not more than food, and the body more than clothing?
Look at the birds of the sky: they neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and yet your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not worth far more than they?
And which of you by worrying can add even eighteen inches{j} to the span of his life?
And why are you anxious about clothing? Study how the wildflowers{k} of the field grow; they do not toil or spin thread,
yet I tell you, not even Solomon in all his splendor was clothed like one of these.
If God so clothes the grass of the field, which is here today and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, will he not much more clothe you, you people of little faith?
Do not fret, then, asking, ‘What will there be to eat?’ or ‘What will there be to drink?’ or ‘What are we going to wear?’
For the Gentiles are eagerly seeking all these things; and your heavenly Father knows that you need them all.
But seek first his kingdom{l} and his righteousness, and all these things will be given to you as well.
So do not be anxious about tomorrow, for tomorrow will have its own anxieties. Each day has trouble enough of its own.

notes.text: Hypocrites: Greek *hypokritai*, “actors,” people who play a part on a stage.
Will reward you: later manuscripts add “openly,” here and in verses 6 and 18; the Westcott–Hort text, with the earliest manuscripts, lacks it.
The bread we need for the day ahead: the rare Greek word *epiousios* may mean “for the coming day,” “for today,” or “necessary for existence.” Its meaning is uncertain.
Debts … in debt to us: sins are pictured as debts owed to God; compare Luke 11:4, “forgive us our sins.”

The evil one: or “evil.” Later manuscripts add a closing doxology: “For yours is the kingdom and the power and the glory forever. Amen.” It is absent from the earliest manuscripts (Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Bezae) and from the earliest commentators on the prayer, and it is not part of the Westcott–Hort text. It is an early liturgical ending, probably modeled on 1 Chr 29:11–13; a shorter form appears in the Didache (8.2, about AD 100). It is therefore given here and not in the text.
Unsightly: literally “make their faces disappear,” perhaps by covering them with ashes or by leaving them unwashed.
Rust: Greek *brōsis*, “eating,” perhaps the corrosion of metal or the gnawing of vermin; also in verse 20.
Healthy: Greek *haplous*, “single,” “sound,” also “generous.” A “diseased” (literally “evil”) eye in verse 23 was an idiom for a stingy or envious disposition.
Wealth: Greek *mamōnas*, from Aramaic *mamona*, “wealth,” “property,” traditionally “mammon.”

Eighteen inches: literally “one cubit,” the length from the elbow to the fingertip, about 18 inches (45 cm). The word for *span of life* (*hēlikia*) can also mean “stature,” but the context concerns length of life; the expression may then mean “a single hour.”
Wildflowers: Greek *krina*, traditionally “lilies,” probably a general term for the bright wildflowers of Galilee.
His kingdom: later manuscripts read “the kingdom of God.”

verses.text: “Do not judge, so that you may not be judged.
For the judgment you pass on others is the judgment that will be passed on you, and the measure you measure out is the measure you will receive.
Why do you notice the speck in your brother’s eye but never notice the log in your own eye?
Or how can you tell your brother, ‘Let me pull the speck out of your eye,’ when all the while there is a log in your own?
You hypocrite, first pull the log out of your own eye, and then you will see well enough to pull the speck from your brother’s eye.
“Do not give what is holy to the dogs, and do not throw your pearls in front of pigs, or they may trample them under their feet and then turn around and tear you to pieces.
“Keep asking, and it will be given you; keep seeking, and you will find; keep knocking, and it will be opened for you.
For all who ask receive; whoever seeks finds; and for whoever knocks, it will be opened.
Is there anyone among you who, if his son asks for bread, will hand him a stone?
Or if he asks for a fish, will hand him a snake?
If you, then, though you are evil, know how to give your children good gifts, how much more will your Father in heaven give good things to those who ask him!
So in everything, treat others in the way you want them to treat you; for this sums up the Law and the Prophets.
“Go in through the narrow gate. For wide is the gate and broad is the road that leads to destruction, and many are those who go in by it.
But how narrow{a} is the gate and how hard is the road that leads to life, and few are those who find it.
“Watch out for false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing but underneath are ravenous wolves.
By their fruit you will know them. Do people pick grapes off thorns, or figs off thistles?
Just so, every healthy tree produces good fruit, but the diseased tree produces bad fruit.
A healthy tree cannot produce bad fruit, nor can a diseased tree produce good fruit.
Any tree that fails to yield good fruit is cut down and cast into the fire.
So it is by their fruit that you will know them.
“It is not all who call me ‘Lord, Lord’ who will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who carries out the will of my Father in heaven.
Many will say to me on that day, ‘Lord, Lord, was it not in your name that we prophesied, in your name that we cast out demons, and in your name that we did many works of power?’
And then I will tell them plainly, ‘I never knew you. Depart from me, you workers of lawlessness.’{b}
“So everyone who hears these words of mine and acts on them will be like a sensible man who built his house on the rock.
The rain came down, the rivers rose, and the winds blew and battered that house, yet it did not fall, because its foundation had been laid on the rock.
And everyone who hears these words of mine and does not act on them will be like a foolish man who built his house on the sand.
The rain came down, the rivers rose, and the winds blew and beat against that house, and it fell, and great was its downfall.”
When Jesus had finished these sayings,{c} the crowds were astounded at his teaching,
for he taught them as one who had authority, and not as their scribes did.

notes.text: How narrow: some manuscripts read “for narrow.” The Westcott–Hort text reads *ti*, “how,” with most witnesses.
When Jesus had finished these sayings: this formula closes each of the five great blocks of Jesus’ teaching in Matthew (7:28; 11:1; 13:53; 19:1; 26:1).

verses.text: When he came down from the mountain, great crowds followed him.
And just then a man with leprosy{a} approached, knelt before him, and said, “Lord, if you are willing, you have the power to make me clean.”
Jesus stretched out his hand and touched him, saying, “I am willing; be made clean.” And immediately his leprosy was cleansed away.
Then Jesus said to him, “Be sure you tell no one; but go and let the priest examine you, and bring the offering that Moses commanded,{b} as evidence to them.”
When he had entered Capernaum, a centurion{c} came up to him and pleaded with him,
“Lord, my servant boy lies paralyzed in the house, suffering dreadfully.”
Jesus answered, “Shall I come and heal him?”{d}
The centurion replied, “Lord, I am not worthy to have you come under my roof. Just say the word, and my servant will be healed.
For I myself am a man placed under authority, with soldiers under me. I say to one, ‘Go,’ and he goes, and to another, ‘Come,’ and he comes, and to my slave, ‘Do this,’ and he does it.”
When Jesus heard it, he marveled, and said to those who were following, “Amen, I tell you, I have not found faith like this from anyone in Israel.{e}
I tell you, many will come from east and west and take their places at the feast with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven,
while the heirs of the kingdom{f} will be thrown out into the darkness outside; there people will weep and grind their teeth.”
Then Jesus said to the centurion, “Go; as you have believed, so let it be done for you.” And his servant was healed at that very hour.
Coming into Peter’s house, Jesus saw that Peter’s wife’s mother was laid up with a fever.
He took hold of her hand, and the fever left her; she rose and began to serve him.
When evening came, people brought to him many who were under the power of demons. He drove out the spirits with a word and healed all who were sick,
so that what was spoken through Isaiah the prophet might be fulfilled: “He himself took away our weaknesses and carried off our diseases.”{g}
When Jesus saw the crowd pressing around him, he ordered a crossing to the far shore.
Then a scribe came up and said to him, “Teacher, I will follow you wherever you are going.”
Jesus told him, “Foxes have dens and the birds of the sky have nests, but the Son of Man{h} has nowhere to rest his head.”
Another of his disciples said to him, “Lord, allow me first to go away and bury my father.”{i}
But Jesus told him, “Follow me, and let the dead bury their own dead.”
He got into the boat, and his disciples went with him.
Without warning a violent storm{j} arose on the lake, so that the boat was being swamped by the waves; but he was sleeping.
They came and woke him, crying, “Lord, save us! We are going to die!”
He said to them, “Why are you so fearful, you people of little faith?” Then he got up and rebuked the winds and the lake, and there was a great calm.
The men were astonished and said, “What sort of man is this, that even the winds and the lake obey him?”
When he reached the other side, the country of the Gadarenes,{k} two men under the power of demons met him, coming out from the tombs. They were so violent that no one could travel along that road.
All at once they shrieked, “What do you want with us, Son of God?{l} Have you come here to torment us before the appointed time?”
Some distance away a large herd of pigs was feeding.
The demons begged him, “If you are going to drive us out, send us into the herd of pigs.”
“Go,” he told them. They came out and went off into the pigs, and the entire herd stampeded down the slope into the lake and drowned.
The herdsmen fled, went off into the town, and reported everything, including what had happened to the men who had been demonized.
And the entire town came out to meet Jesus; and when they saw him, they pleaded with him to leave their district.

notes.text: Leprosy: the Greek word covered a range of skin diseases (see Lev 13–14), not only Hansen’s disease. Such a person was ritually unclean and excluded from community life.
Centurion: a Roman officer in command of about a hundred soldiers; this one, stationed in Galilee, was probably serving Herod Antipas and was a Gentile.
Am I to come and heal him?: or, as a statement, “I will come and heal him.” The Greek can be read either way.
With no one in Israel …: some manuscripts read “not even in Israel have I found such faith.” The Westcott–Hort text follows Vaticanus and other early witnesses.
Heirs of the kingdom: literally “sons of the kingdom,” those who would be expected to inherit it.
Isa 53:4, translated from the Hebrew.
Son of Man: Jesus’ preferred way of referring to himself. In Aramaic the phrase can mean simply “a human being” (compare Ps 8:4; Ezek 2:1), but it also recalls the heavenly figure of Dan 7:13–14.
Bury my father: this may mean that the man’s father had just died, or that he wished to wait until his father died and he had received his inheritance.
Violent storm: Greek *seismos megas*, literally “a great shaking,” the word normally used for an earthquake.

Gadarenes: the people of Gadara, a city of the Ten Towns about 6 miles (10 km) southeast of the lake. Manuscripts vary: the Westcott–Hort text reads *Gadarenes* with Vaticanus; others read *Gerasenes* (as in Mark 5:1) or *Gergesenes*. Scholarly review recommended.
Son of God: later manuscripts add “Jesus.”

verses.text: He stepped into a boat, crossed the lake, and came to his own town.{a}
And there they brought him a man who was paralyzed, laid on a stretcher. Seeing their faith, Jesus told the paralyzed man, “Courage, my son; your sins are forgiven.”
At this some of the scribes said to themselves, “This man is blaspheming.”
Jesus, knowing{b} what they were thinking, said, “Why do you think evil things in your hearts?
Which is easier: to say, ‘Your sins are forgiven,’ or to say, ‘Get up and walk’?
But so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins”—he then said to the paralyzed man—“Get up, pick up your mat, and go home.”
And the man got up and went off home.
The crowds who saw it were struck with awe,{c} and they glorified God for giving such authority to mortals.
As Jesus went on from there, he saw a man named Matthew{d} sitting at the tax booth, and he said to him, “Follow me.” And he got up and followed him.
Later, as Jesus was reclining at table in the house,{e} many tax collectors and sinners came and joined Jesus and his disciples at the meal.
Seeing this, the Pharisees said to his disciples, “Why does your teacher eat with tax collectors and sinners?”
He heard them and said, “It is not the healthy who have need of a doctor, but the sick.
Go and find out what this means: ‘It is mercy I desire, and not sacrifice.’{f} For I did not come to call the righteous, but sinners.”
Then John’s disciples came to him and asked, “Why is it that we and the Pharisees fast often,{g} but your disciples do not fast?”
Jesus answered them, “Can the bridegroom’s friends{h} mourn while he is still with them? But days are coming when the bridegroom will be taken from them, and then they will fast.
Nobody sews a patch of unshrunk cloth on an old garment; the patch would pull away from the garment, and a worse tear would result.

Nor do people pour new wine into old wineskins;{i} if they do, the skins split open, the wine pours out, and the skins are ruined. Instead they pour new wine into fresh wineskins, and both are kept safe.”
While he was saying these things to them, a leader{j} came in, knelt before him, and said, “My daughter has just died; but come and lay your hand on her, and she will live.”
So Jesus rose and followed him, together with his disciples.
Then a woman who had suffered from bleeding for twelve years came up behind him and touched the tassel{k} of his cloak.
She had been telling herself, “If I can just touch his cloak, I will be healed.”
Jesus turned, and when he saw her, he said, “Courage, daughter! Your faith has made you whole.” And from that very hour the woman was whole.
When Jesus came into the leader’s house and saw the flute players{l} and the crowd making a commotion,
he told them, “Leave; the girl has not died, she is sleeping.” They ridiculed him.
But once the crowd had been put outside, he went in and took her by the hand, and the girl rose up.
And the news of this spread through that whole region.
As Jesus went on from there, two blind men followed him, crying out, “Have mercy on us, Son of David!”{m}
When he had gone indoors, the blind men came to him, and Jesus asked them, “Do you believe that I am able to do this?” They told him, “Yes, Lord.”
Then he touched their eyes and said, “Be it done to you in keeping with your faith.”{n}
And their eyes were opened. Jesus gave them a stern warning, “See that no one learns of this.”
But they went out and made him known throughout that whole district.
As they were leaving, some people brought to him a man who could not speak because of a demon.
And when the demon had been driven out, the mute man spoke. The crowds were amazed and said, “Nothing like this has ever been seen in Israel.”
[But the Pharisees were saying, “It is by the ruler of the demons that he drives out the demons.”]{o}
Jesus went around all the towns and villages, teaching in their synagogues, proclaiming the good news of the kingdom, and healing every disease and every ailment.
Seeing the crowds, he was moved with compassion for them, because they were worn out and helpless, like sheep with no shepherd.{p}
Then he told his disciples, “The harvest is great, but the laborers are few.
Ask the Lord of the harvest, then, to send out workers into his harvest.”

notes.text: His own town: Capernaum (4:13).
Knowing: many manuscripts read “seeing,” which the Westcott–Hort text places in the margin.
Filled with awe: literally “they were afraid.” Later manuscripts read “they marveled.”
Matthew: from Hebrew *Mattithyah*, “gift of Yahweh.” In Mark 2:14 and Luke 5:27 the tax collector is called Levi; the Gospel bearing his name was attributed to him from the second century.
In the house: probably Matthew’s house (compare Luke 5:29), though the Greek may mean Jesus’ own house. At formal meals guests reclined on couches, leaning on the left elbow.
Hos 6:6, quoted again in 12:7.
Fast often: the Westcott–Hort text, with the first hand of Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, lacks “often,” which it places in the margin; most manuscripts include it.
The bridegroom’s friends: literally “the sons of the bridal chamber,” the wedding guests.
Wineskins: containers made from the whole skin of a goat. New wine continued to ferment and swell, and old skins, already stretched, would burst.
A leader: Greek *archōn*, “ruler,” probably the leader of a synagogue; Mark 5:22 names him Jairus.
Tassel: the fringe worn at the corners of the outer garment in obedience to Num 15:38–41 and Deut 22:12.
Flute players: professional mourners and musicians were customarily hired for funerals.
Son of David: a title for the Messiah, the promised heir of David’s throne (2 Sam 7:12–16; Isa 11:1–10).
In keeping with your faith: literally “according to your faith.”

This verse is absent from some Western witnesses (Codex Bezae, some Old Latin manuscripts, and the Sinaitic Syriac), and Westcott and Hort placed it in single brackets as doubtful. It is present in all other manuscripts, including Sinaiticus and Vaticanus. Compare 12:24.
Like sheep with no shepherd: compare Num 27:17; 1 Kgs 22:17; Ezek 34:5.

verses.text: Jesus summoned his twelve disciples and gave them authority over unclean spirits, to drive them out, and to heal every disease and every ailment.
These are the names of the twelve apostles:{a} first, Simon, who is called Peter, and Andrew his brother; James son of Zebedee, and John his brother;
Philip and Bartholomew; Thomas and Matthew the tax collector; James son of Alphaeus, and Thaddaeus;{b}
Simon the Cananaean,{c} and Judas Iscariot,{d} who also betrayed him.
These twelve Jesus sent out with these instructions: “Do not go off onto the roads of the Gentiles, and do not go into any Samaritan town.{e}
Go instead to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.
As you travel, make this announcement: ‘The kingdom of heaven is close at hand.’
Heal the sick, raise the dead,{f} make lepers clean, drive out demons. You received without paying; give without being paid.
Take no gold, no silver, no copper in your belts,
nor a bag for the journey, nor two shirts, nor sandals, nor a staff, for the worker deserves to be fed.{g}
Whatever town or village you enter, find out who in it is worthy, and stay with him until you leave.
As you go into the house, give it your greeting.{h}
If the house is worthy, let your peace come upon it; but if it is not, let your peace return to you.
And if anyone will not welcome you or listen to your words, then when you leave that house or town, shake its dust off your feet.{i}
Amen, I tell you, on the day of judgment it will be more bearable for the land of Sodom and Gomorrah than for that town.
“See, I send you out as sheep into the midst of wolves. Be wary, then, as serpents are, and guileless, as doves are.
Be on your guard against people, for they will hand you over to local councils and flog you in their synagogues;
You will even be brought before governors and kings for my sake, as a testimony to them and to the nations.
But when they deliver you up, do not be anxious over how you will speak or what you will say, for in that hour you will be given what to say.
For it is not you who speak; it is the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you.
One brother will deliver another up to death, and a father his child; children will rise in revolt against parents and cause their deaths;{j}
and you will be hated by everyone because of my name. But the one who holds out to the end will be saved.
Whenever they persecute you in one town, escape to the next; amen, I tell you, before you have completed the circuit of Israel’s towns, the Son of Man will come.
“A disciple is not above his teacher, nor a slave above his master.
The disciple should be satisfied to be like his teacher, and the slave like his master. If they named the master of the house Beelzebul,{k} how much worse names will they give those of his household!
“So do not be afraid of them; for there is nothing covered that will not be uncovered, and nothing hidden that will not be made known.
What I tell you in the dark, speak in the daylight; and what you hear whispered in your ear, proclaim from the housetops.
Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul. Fear rather the one who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna.
Are not two sparrows sold for a single small coin?{l} Yet not one of them will fall to the ground apart from your Father.
And as for you, every hair of your head has been numbered.
So do not be afraid; you are of more value than a great many sparrows.
“Whoever, then, acknowledges me before others, I too will acknowledge before my Father in heaven;
but whoever disowns me before others, I too will disown before my Father in heaven.
“Do not suppose that I came to bring peace upon the earth. I did not come to bring peace, but a sword.
For I came to set a man against his father, a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law;
a man will find his enemies among those of his own house.{m}
Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me, and whoever loves son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me.
And whoever does not take up his cross and follow after me is not worthy of me.
Whoever has found his life will lose it, and whoever has lost his life because of me will find it.
“To receive you is to receive me, and to receive me is to receive the one who sent me.
Anyone who receives a prophet as a prophet will get a prophet’s reward, and anyone who receives a righteous person as a righteous person will get a righteous person’s reward.
And whoever gives even a cup of cold water to one of these little ones because he is a disciple, amen, I tell you, that person will certainly not lose his reward.”

notes.text: Apostles: Greek *apostoloi*, “those sent out,” “envoys.” *Philip* is a Greek name meaning “lover of horses.” *Bartholomew* is Aramaic for “son of Tolmai” (or “of Talmai”).

Thomas … Thaddaeus: *Thomas* is from Aramaic *teʾoma*, “twin” (see John 11:16). *Alphaeus* is probably from Aramaic *Halfai*. *Thaddaeus* is perhaps from Aramaic *tad*, “breast,” meaning something like “beloved.” Some manuscripts read *Lebbaeus*, or “Lebbaeus who was called Thaddaeus”; the Westcott–Hort text reads *Thaddaeus*. Luke 6:16 and Acts 1:13 have “Judas son of James” in his place.
Cananaean: from Aramaic *qanʾan*, “zealous one,” not a reference to Canaan. Luke 6:15 calls him “the Zealot.”
Iscariot: probably Hebrew *ish Qeriyyot*, “man of Kerioth,” a town in southern Judea (Josh 15:25); other explanations have been proposed. *Judas* is the Greek form of *Judah*, “praised” (Gen 29:35).
Samaritan: the people of Samaria, between Judea and Galilee, who worshiped the God of Israel at Mount Gerizim and accepted only the five books of Moses. Jews and Samaritans were bitterly estranged.
Raise the dead: some later manuscripts omit these words.
Deserves to be fed: literally “is worthy of his food.” Compare Luke 10:7; 1 Tim 5:18.
Give it your greeting: the customary greeting was *shalom*, “peace” (verse 13). Some manuscripts add, “saying, ‘Peace to this house.’ ”
Shake its dust off your feet: a sign of disowning a place; devout Jews were said to do this when returning from Gentile territory.
Compare Mic 7:6.

Beelzebul: a name for the prince of demons (12:24), probably “lord of the dwelling” or “lord of the heights,” perhaps a deliberate twist of *Baal-zebub*, “lord of flies,” the god of Ekron (2 Kgs 1:2). Later manuscripts read *Beelzebub*.
A single small coin: Greek *assarion*, a Roman copper coin worth one sixteenth of a denarius (a day’s wage), roughly what a laborer earned in forty minutes.
Mic 7:6.

verses.text: Once Jesus had completed his charge to the Twelve, he left that place and went on teaching and proclaiming in the towns of the region.
Word reached John in his prison cell about the works of the Messiah, and he dispatched his disciples
with a question: “Is it you who are the Coming One, or must we wait for a different person?”
Jesus replied, “Go back and tell John what you are hearing and seeing:
the blind regain their sight and the lame walk about, those with leprosy are made clean and the deaf hear, the dead are raised, and the poor are hearing good news.{a}
Happy is the one who finds in me no cause for stumbling.”
While they were on their way, Jesus spoke to the crowds concerning John: “When you trekked out into the wilderness, what were you expecting to look at? A reed shaken by the wind?
What, then, did you go out to see? Someone dressed in soft, fine clothing? Look, those who wear fine clothing are to be found in royal palaces.
Then what did you go out for? To see a prophet? Yes, I tell you, and one who is more than a prophet.
He is the man of whom Scripture says, ‘Look, I send my messenger before your face; he will make your road ready ahead of you.’{b}
Amen, I tell you, among all born of women there has never arisen anyone greater than John the Baptist; yet the one who is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he.
From the days of John the Baptist until now the kingdom of heaven has been under violent attack, and violent people are trying to seize it.{c}
For all the Prophets and the Law prophesied until John;
and if you are willing to accept it, he himself is Elijah, who was to come.{d}
Whoever has ears, let him hear.
“But to what shall I compare this generation? It is like children sitting in the marketplaces who call out to the others,
‘We played the flute for you, and you would not dance; we sang a dirge, and you would not beat your breasts.’
For John came neither eating nor drinking, and they say, ‘He has a demon.’
The Son of Man came eating and drinking, and they say, ‘There goes a glutton and a wine-drinker, a crony of tax collectors and sinners!’ Yet wisdom is shown to be right by what she does.”{e}
Then he began to denounce the towns in which most of his mighty works had been done, because they had not changed their ways.
“Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida!{f} For if the mighty works done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon,{g} they would have turned from their sins long ago, in sackcloth and ashes.
But I tell you, Tyre and Sidon will find the day of judgment more bearable than you will.
And you, Capernaum, will you be lifted up as high as heaven? You will be brought down as low as Hades.{h} For if the mighty works done in you had been done in Sodom, it would still be standing today.
But I tell you that the land of Sodom will find the day of judgment more bearable than you will.”
At that time Jesus spoke up and said, “I give you praise, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and learned and have revealed them to little children.
Yes, Father, for this is what pleased you.
All things have been put into my hands by my Father. None knows the Son fully except the Father; none knows the Father fully except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son is pleased to make him known.
“Come to me, all who are weary and weighed down, and I will give you rest.
Take my yoke{i} upon you and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls.{j}
For my yoke is kindly and my load is light.”

notes.text: Mal 3:1; compare Exod 23:20. In Malachi the messenger prepares the way “before me,” that is, before Yahweh.

Has been under violent attack … seize it: the Greek is difficult. It may also mean “the kingdom of heaven has been forcefully advancing, and forceful people are laying hold of it.” Scholarly review recommended.
Elijah, who was to come: see Mal 4:5–6 (3:23–24 in Hebrew). *Elijah* means “my God is Yahweh.”
By what she does: literally “by her deeds.” The Westcott–Hort text, with Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, reads *ergōn*, “deeds”; most later manuscripts read “by her children,” as in Luke 7:35.
Chorazin … Bethsaida: towns on or near the northern shore of the Sea of Galilee, close to Capernaum. *Bethsaida* means “house of fishing.”
Tyre and Sidon: Gentile seaports on the Phoenician coast, denounced by the prophets (Isa 23; Ezek 26–28).
Hades: the Greek name for the realm of the dead, corresponding to Hebrew *Sheol*. Compare Isa 14:13–15.
Yoke: the wooden frame laid on the necks of draft animals; in Jewish usage, a figure for submission to the Law or to the teaching of a rabbi.

verses.text: About that time, on a Sabbath day, Jesus was walking through fields of grain.{a} His disciples were hungry, and they started to pluck the ears and eat them.
The Pharisees saw it and told him, “See there! Your disciples are doing what the Sabbath does not allow.”
He said to them, “Have you never read what David did when he and his companions were hungry,
how he went into the house of God and they ate the consecrated bread,{b} which neither he nor his companions were permitted to eat, but only the priests?{c}
Or have you never read in the Law that on the Sabbath the priests in the temple break the Sabbath and yet are blameless?{d}
I tell you, here is something greater than the temple.
If you had grasped what this means, ‘It is mercy I desire, and not sacrifice,’{e} you would not have condemned the innocent.
For the Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath.”
Moving on from there, he went into their synagogue.
A man was there with a shriveled hand. Looking for a charge to bring against Jesus, they asked him, “Is healing on the Sabbath permitted?”
He said to them, “Suppose one of you has a single sheep and it tumbles into a pit on the Sabbath: will he not grab it and pull it out?
A man is worth so much more than a sheep! It is lawful, then, to do good on Sabbath days.”
Then he said to the man, “Hold out your hand.” He held it out, and it was restored, as sound as the other.
But the Pharisees went out and plotted against him, how they might do away with him.
Jesus knew of this and withdrew from there. Many{f} followed him, and he healed them all,
and he sternly ordered them not to make him known.
This was to fulfill what was spoken through Isaiah the prophet:
“Here is my servant, whom I have chosen, my beloved, in whom my soul delights. I will put my Spirit upon him, and he will announce justice to the nations.
He will not quarrel or shout, nor will anyone hear his voice in the streets.
He will not snap a bent reed, nor quench a flickering wick, till he has led justice on to victory.
And in his name the nations will put their hope.”{g}
Then they brought him a man under a demon’s power, blind and mute, and Jesus healed him, so that he spoke and saw.
The crowds, all of them amazed, kept saying, “Might this man be the Son of David?”
Hearing this, the Pharisees said, “It is only through Beelzebul, prince of the demons, that this fellow casts the demons out.”
Knowing their thoughts, Jesus said to them, “Any kingdom split against itself ends in ruin, and any town or family split against itself cannot last.
If Satan drives out Satan, he is divided against himself; how then will his kingdom stand?
And if it is through Beelzebul that I cast out demons, through whom do your own people{h} cast them out? They, then, will be your judges.
But if I cast the demons out through God’s Spirit, the kingdom of God has arrived among you.
Or how can anyone go into a strong man’s house and carry off his goods, unless he first ties up the strong man? Only then will he plunder his house.
Anyone not on my side opposes me, and anyone not gathering with me is scattering.
“So I say to you: every sin and blasphemy people commit will be forgiven, but blasphemy against the Spirit will find no forgiveness.{i}
Someone who says something against the Son of Man will be forgiven, but someone who speaks against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, not in this age, and not in the one to come.
“Either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree rotten and its fruit rotten; for the tree is known by its fruit.
You brood of vipers, how can you say anything good when you are evil? For the mouth speaks out of what overflows from the heart.
A good person, from the good stored up within, brings out good; an evil person, from the evil stored up within, brings out evil.
I tell you, every thoughtless word that people utter they will answer for on judgment day;
for by your words you will be acquitted, and by your words you will be condemned.”
Then some of the scribes and Pharisees responded to him, “Teacher, we want to see a sign from you.”
He answered them, “An evil and adulterous{j} generation demands a sign, but no sign will be given to it except the sign of Jonah the prophet.{k}
For just as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the sea monster,{l} so will the Son of Man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth.
On judgment day the people of Nineveh will rise with this generation and pronounce it guilty, for they turned from their ways when Jonah preached; and here is something greater than Jonah.

The queen of the South{m} will rise up at the judgment with this generation and condemn it, because she came from the ends of the earth to listen to Solomon’s wisdom; and look, something greater than Solomon is here.
“When an unclean spirit has gone out of a person, it roams through waterless places seeking rest, and finds none.
Then it says, ‘I will go back to my house that I left.’ And when it comes, it finds the house empty, swept clean, and put in order.

Then off it goes and fetches seven more spirits, worse than itself, and they move in and make their home there; and that person ends up in a worse state than at the start. So it will be with this wicked generation too.”
He was still talking with the crowds when his mother and brothers{n} came and stood outside, seeking to speak to him.
[Someone said to him, “Your mother and brothers are out there, and they want a word with you.”]{o}
But he replied to the one who told him, “Who is my mother, and who are my brothers?”
Then he pointed to his disciples and said, “See, these are my mother and my brothers!
For whoever does the will of my Father in heaven is my brother and sister and mother.”

notes.text: Sabbath: from Hebrew *shabbat*, “ceasing,” “rest,” the seventh day of the week (Friday sunset to Saturday sunset), on which work was forbidden (Exod 20:8–11). Picking grain by hand from a neighbor’s field was allowed (Deut 23:25), but the Pharisees counted it as reaping, a kind of work.
Consecrated bread: literally “the bread of the presentation,” the twelve loaves set out each week before God in the sanctuary (Lev 24:5–9).
Hos 6:6; see 9:13.
Many: the Westcott–Hort text, with Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, reads “many”; later manuscripts read “great crowds.”
Isa 42:1–4, quoted freely, partly following the Hebrew and partly the Greek Old Testament (verse 21).
Your own people: literally “your sons,” that is, Jewish exorcists associated with the Pharisees.
Blasphemy against the Spirit: attributing to Satan the work that God’s Spirit is plainly doing (12:24, 28).
Adulterous: unfaithful to God, as in the prophets’ picture of Israel as an unfaithful wife (Hos 2; Ezek 16).
Jonah: “dove.” See the book of Jonah, especially 1:17 and 3:5.
Sea monster: Greek *kētos*, “huge fish” or “sea creature” (Jonah 1:17 in the Greek Old Testament).
The queen of the South: the queen of Sheba, probably in southwest Arabia (1 Kgs 10:1–10).
His brothers: named in 13:55. Catholic and Orthodox tradition understands them as cousins or as children of Joseph by an earlier marriage.

The Westcott–Hort text, with the first hand of Sinaiticus, Vaticanus and a few other witnesses, omits this verse, placing it in the margin; most manuscripts include it, and it is needed to make sense of verse 48. It is printed here in brackets.

verses.text: That same day Jesus went out of the house and sat down beside the lake.
So many people crowded around him that he stepped into a boat and sat down in it, and all the people stood along the beach.
He spoke to them at length in parables.{a} “Listen,” he said. “A sower went out to scatter seed.
As he scattered it, some fell beside the path, and birds swooped down and devoured it.
Other seed fell on rocky places where it did not have much soil, and it sprang up at once because the soil was shallow;
When the sun rose, the young plants were scorched and, having no root, dried up.
Other seed fell among thornbushes, and the thorns grew up and choked it.
Still other seed fell on good soil and yielded a crop, some a hundred times as much, some sixty, some thirty.
Whoever has ears, let him hear.”
The disciples approached him and said, “Why are you talking to them in parables?”
He replied, “You have been granted knowledge of the secrets{b} of the kingdom of heaven; they have not.
For whoever has, more will be given him, and he will have an abundance; but whoever has nothing, even what he has will be taken from him.
This is why I speak to them in parables: because seeing they do not see, and hearing they do not hear or understand.
In them the prophecy of Isaiah is being fulfilled, which says, ‘You will listen and listen, yet never understand; you will look and look, yet never perceive.

For this people’s heart has grown dull; with their ears they barely hear, and they have shut their eyes, so that they may not see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their heart, and turn back, and I would heal them.’{c}
But blessed are your eyes, because they see, and your ears, because they hear.
Amen, I tell you, many prophets and righteous people yearned to see the things you see, but never saw them, and to hear the things you hear, but never heard them.
“Listen, then, to what the parable of the sower means.
When anyone hears the word of the kingdom and does not understand it, the evil one comes and snatches away what was sown in his heart; this is the seed sown along the path.
The seed sown on rocky places is the one who hears the word and at once receives it with joy;
but he has no root in himself and lasts only a short while, and when trouble or persecution comes because of the word, he immediately falls away.
The seed sown among the thorns is the one who hears the word, but the cares of this age and the lure of wealth choke the word, and it yields nothing.
But the seed sown on the good soil is the one who hears the word and understands it; he indeed bears fruit and yields, one a hundredfold, another sixty, another thirty.”
He set another parable before them: “The kingdom of heaven is like this. A man sowed good seed in his field.
But while everyone was asleep, his enemy came and sowed darnel{d} among the wheat and went away.
When the wheat sprouted and formed heads of grain, then the darnel appeared too.
The owner’s slaves came to him and said, ‘Sir, did you not sow good seed in your field? Where then did the darnel come from?’
He told them, ‘An enemy has done this.’ The slaves asked him, ‘Do you want us, then, to go and pull it up?’
But he said, ‘No; in pulling up the darnel you might uproot the wheat along with it.
Let both grow side by side until the harvest; and at harvest time I will tell the reapers, Collect the darnel first and tie it in bundles to be burned, but gather the wheat into my barn.’ ”
He put before them another parable: “The kingdom of heaven is like a mustard seed, which a man took and sowed in his field.
Of all seeds it is the tiniest, yet when full grown it is bigger than any garden plant; it becomes a tree, and the birds of the sky come and make their nests among its branches.”{e}
He told them another parable: “The kingdom of heaven is like yeast that a woman took and worked into about fifty pounds of flour{f} until the whole batch was leavened.”
Jesus told the crowds all these things in parables; indeed, he told them nothing without a parable.
This fulfilled what was spoken through the prophet:{g} “I will open my mouth in parables; I will pour out things hidden since the foundation of the world.”{h}
Then he left the crowds and went into the house. His disciples came to him and said, “Explain to us the parable of the darnel in the field.”
He answered, “The one who sows the good seed is the Son of Man.
The field is the world; the good seed stands for the children of the kingdom; the darnel stands for the children of the evil one;
the enemy who sowed it is the devil; the harvest is the end of the age; and the reapers are angels.
Just as the darnel is gathered and burned up in the fire, so will it be at the end of the age.
The Son of Man will send out his angels, and they will gather out of his kingdom all who cause others to sin and all who do evil,
and they will throw them into the blazing furnace; there people will weep and grind their teeth.
Then the righteous will shine like the sun in their Father’s kingdom.{i} Whoever has ears, let him hear.
“The kingdom of heaven is like treasure buried in a field, which a man found and buried again; then in his joy he goes and sells everything he has and buys that field.
“Or again, the kingdom of heaven is like a trader on the lookout for beautiful pearls.
When he found one pearl of great price, he went away and sold everything he had and bought it.
“Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a dragnet that was let down into the lake and caught fish of every kind.
When it was full, they hauled it onto the shore, sat down, and collected the good fish into containers, but threw away the worthless ones.
So it will be at the end of the age. The angels will go out and separate the wicked from the righteous
and throw them into the blazing furnace; there people will weep and grind their teeth.
“Have you understood all this?” They said to him, “Yes.”
And he said to them, “So then, every scribe who has been trained as a disciple for the kingdom of heaven resembles a householder who brings out of his storehouse things new and things old.”
When Jesus had finished these parables, he left that place.
Coming to his hometown,{j} he taught the people in their synagogue, and they were astounded and said, “Where did this man get this wisdom and these mighty powers?
This is the carpenter’s son,{k} is he not? His mother is Mary, isn’t she, and his brothers are James, Joseph,{l} Simon and Judas?
And are not all his sisters here with us? Where then did he get all this?”
And they took offense at him. But Jesus said to them, “A prophet is not without honor except in his hometown and in his own house.”
And he did not do many mighty works there because of their unbelief.

notes.text: Parables: Greek *parabolē*, “comparison,” corresponding to Hebrew *mashal*, a saying, proverb, riddle or illustrative story.
Secrets: Greek *mystēria*, things hidden in God’s purpose and now revealed.
Isa 6:9–10, quoted in the wording of the Greek Old Testament.
Darnel: Greek *zizania*, a weed (*Lolium temulentum*) that closely resembles wheat until it forms its head. Its seeds are bitter and mildly poisonous. Traditionally “tares.”
The birds … nest in its branches: compare Ps 104:12; Ezek 17:23; 31:6; Dan 4:12, 21.

About fifty pounds of flour: literally “three *sata*” of flour. A *saton* (Hebrew *seah*) was about 13 quarts (12–13 liters), so the total was about 10 gallons (39 liters), enough bread for well over a hundred people. Compare Gen 18:6.
The prophet: a few manuscripts, including the first hand of Sinaiticus, read “Isaiah the prophet”; the quotation is from Asaph (Ps 78), whom 2 Chr 29:30 calls a seer.
Compare Dan 12:3.
His hometown: Nazareth (2:23).
Carpenter: Greek *tektōn*, a craftsman who worked in wood or stone, a builder.
Joseph: later manuscripts read *Joses* (as in Mark 6:3) or *John*. *James* is *Jacob* (see 4:21 note); *Judas* is *Judah*.

verses.text: At that time Herod the tetrarch{a} heard the reports about Jesus,
and he said to his servants, “This is John the Baptist; he has been raised from the dead! That is why these powers are at work in him.”
For Herod had arrested John, bound him, and put him in prison on account of Herodias, the wife of his brother Philip,{b}
because John had been telling him, “It is against the law for you to have her.”{c}
Herod wanted to put him to death, but he was afraid of the people, because they regarded John as a prophet.
But on Herod’s birthday, the daughter of Herodias{d} danced before the guests, and Herod was so delighted
that he swore an oath to give her whatever she asked.
Prompted by her mother, she said, “Give me here on a platter the head of John the Baptist.”
The king was grieved, but because of his oaths and his guests he ordered it to be given her.
He sent orders, and John was beheaded in the prison.
His head was brought on a platter and given to the girl, and she brought it to her mother.
Then John’s disciples came and took away the body and buried it, and went and told Jesus.
When Jesus heard it, he withdrew from there by boat to a deserted place to be by himself. But the crowds learned of it and followed him on foot from the towns.
When he came ashore, he saw a great crowd, and he was moved with compassion for them and healed their sick.

With evening approaching, the disciples came to him. “This is a lonely spot,” they said, “and the day is far gone. Let the people go, so that they can make their way to the villages and get provisions for themselves.”
But Jesus said, “There is no need for them to leave. You yourselves give them food.”
They said to him, “All we have here are five loaves and two fish.”
He said, “Bring them here to me.”

Then he directed the crowds to sit down on the grass. He took the five loaves and the two fish, and looking up to heaven he said a blessing; he broke the loaves and gave them to the disciples, and the disciples gave them to the crowds.
Everyone ate and was satisfied, and they gathered up what was left over of the broken pieces, twelve baskets full.
Those who ate were about five thousand men, besides women and children.
Immediately he made the disciples get into the boat and go on ahead of him to the other side, while he sent the crowds away.
When he had dismissed them, he climbed the mountain alone to pray. Evening fell, and he was there by himself,
but the boat was by this time a long way from land,{e} being battered by the waves, for the wind was against it.
Between three and six in the morning{f} he came toward them, walking on the lake.
When the disciples saw him walking on the lake, they were terrified and said, “It is a ghost!” and they cried out in fear.
But at once Jesus spoke to them: “Take heart; it is I.{g} Do not be afraid.”
Peter answered him, “Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you on the water.”
“Come,” said Jesus. Peter climbed out of the boat and walked on the water, making his way toward Jesus.
But when he saw the wind,{h} he became frightened, and beginning to sink, he cried out, “Lord, save me!”
Jesus immediately reached out his hand and caught hold of him, saying to him, “You of little faith, why did you doubt?”
And when they had climbed into the boat, the wind died down.
Those in the boat bowed down before him and said, “Truly you are the Son of God.”
When they had crossed over, they came to land at Gennesaret.{i}
When the men of that place recognized him, they sent word into all that surrounding region and brought to him all who were sick,
and they begged him that they might merely touch the tassel of his cloak; and all who touched it were made completely well.

notes.text: Herod the tetrarch: Herod Antipas, son of Herod the Great, ruler of Galilee and Perea from 4 BC to AD 39. *Tetrarch* (“ruler of a fourth”) was a title for a minor ruler under Rome; Matthew also calls him “king” (verse 9).

Herodias … Philip: Herodias was a granddaughter of Herod the Great. She had been married to her uncle Herod (called Philip here and in Mark 6:17), and left him to marry his half-brother Antipas. Some manuscripts omit “Philip.” The historian Josephus gives a fuller account (*Antiquities* 18.5).
Against the law: Lev 18:16; 20:21.
The daughter of Herodias: named Salome by Josephus.

A long way from land: literally “many stadia from the land.” A stadion was about 607 feet (185 m). The Westcott–Hort text follows Vaticanus here; other manuscripts read “in the middle of the lake.” Compare John 6:19, “about 25 or 30 stadia,” about 3 or 3½ miles (5 or 6 km).
Between three and six in the morning: literally “in the fourth watch of the night.” The Romans divided the night into four watches: about 6–9 p.m., 9 p.m.–midnight, midnight–3 a.m., and 3–6 a.m.
It is I: Greek *egō eimi*, literally “I am,” which may echo God’s self-identification in Exod 3:14 and Isa 43:10.
Saw the wind: the Westcott–Hort text, with Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, lacks “strong,” which most manuscripts add.
Gennesaret: a fertile plain on the northwest shore of the Sea of Galilee, between Capernaum and Magdala.
